{{Short description|"Pushed forward" from one measurable space to another}}
{{More citations needed|date=June 2025}}
In [[measure theory]], a '''pushforward measure''' (also known as '''push forward''', '''push-forward''' or '''image measure''') is obtained by transferring ("pushing forward") a [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] from one [[measurable space]] to another using a [[measurable function]].

==Definition==
Given [[Measurable space|measurable spaces]] <math>(X_1,\Sigma_1)</math> and <math>(X_2,\Sigma_2)</math>, a [[measurable function]] <math>f\colon X_1\to X_2</math> and a measure <math>\mu\colon\Sigma_1\to[0,+\infty]</math>, the '''pushforward''' of <math>\mu</math> by <math>f</math> is defined to be the measure <math>f_{*}(\mu)\colon\Sigma_2\to[0,+\infty]</math> given by

:<math>f_{*} (\mu) (B) = \mu \left( f^{-1} (B) \right)</math> for <math>B \in \Sigma_{2}.</math>

This definition applies ''[[mutatis mutandis]]'' for a [[signed measure|signed]] or [[complex measure]].
The pushforward measure is also denoted as <math>\mu \circ f^{-1}</math>, <math>f_\sharp \mu</math>, <math>f \sharp \mu</math>, or <math>f \# \mu</math>.

==Properties==

===Change of variable formula===

Theorem:<ref>Theorem 3.6.1 in {{Harvnb|Bogachev|2007}}</ref> A measurable function ''g'' on ''X''<sub>2</sub> is integrable with respect to the pushforward measure ''f''<sub>∗</sub>(''μ'') if and only if the composition <math>g \circ f</math> is integrable with respect to the  measure ''μ''. In that case, the integrals coincide, i.e.,

:<math>\int_{X_2} g \, d(f_* \mu) = \int_{X_1} g \circ f \, d\mu.</math>

Note that in the previous formula <math>X_1=f^{-1}(X_2)</math>.

===Functoriality===

Pushforwards of measures allow to induce, from a function between [[measurable space]]s <math>f:X\to Y</math>, a function between the spaces of measures <math>M(X)\to M(Y)</math>.
As with many induced mappings, this construction has the structure of a [[functor]], on the [[category of measurable spaces]].

For the special case of [[probability measure]]s, this property amounts to functoriality of the [[Giry monad]].

==Examples and applications==
* If <math> (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P) </math> is a [[probability space]], <math> (E, \mathcal{E}) </math> is a [[measurable space]], and <math> X : \Omega \to E </math> is a <math> (E, \mathcal{E}) </math>-valued random variable, then the [[probability distribution]] of <math>X</math> is the pushforward measure of <math>P</math> by <math>X</math> onto <math> (E, \mathcal{E}) </math>.
* A natural "[[Lebesgue measure]]" on the [[unit circle]] '''S'''<sup>1</sup> (here thought of as a subset of the [[complex plane]] '''C''') may be defined using a push-forward construction and Lebesgue measure ''λ'' on the [[real line]] '''R'''. Let ''λ'' also denote the restriction of Lebesgue measure to the interval [0,&nbsp;2''π'') and let ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;2''π'')&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''S'''<sup>1</sup> be the natural bijection defined by ''f''(''t'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;exp(''i''&nbsp;''t''). The natural "Lebesgue measure" on '''S'''<sup>1</sup> is then the push-forward measure ''f''<sub>∗</sub>(''λ''). The measure ''f''<sub>∗</sub>(''λ'') might also be called "[[arc length]] measure" or "angle measure", since the ''f''<sub>∗</sub>(''λ'')-measure of an arc in '''S'''<sup>1</sup> is precisely its arc length (or, equivalently, the angle that it subtends at the centre of the circle.)
* The previous example extends nicely to give a natural "Lebesgue measure" on the ''n''-dimensional [[torus]] '''T'''<sup>''n''</sup>. The previous example is a special case, since '''S'''<sup>1</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;'''T'''<sup>1</sup>. This Lebesgue measure on '''T'''<sup>''n''</sup> is, up to normalization, the [[Haar measure]] for the [[compact space|compact]], [[connected space|connected]] [[Lie group]] '''T'''<sup>''n''</sup>.
* [[Gaussian measure]]s on infinite-dimensional vector spaces are defined using the push-forward and the standard Gaussian measure on the real line: a [[Borel measure]] ''γ'' on a [[separable space|separable]] [[Banach space]] ''X'' is called '''Gaussian''' if the push-forward of ''γ'' by any non-zero [[linear functional]] in the [[continuous dual space]] to ''X'' is a Gaussian measure on '''R'''.
* Consider a measurable function ''f'' : ''X'' → ''X'' and the [[Function composition|composition]] of ''f'' with itself ''n'' times:

::<math>f^{(n)} = \underbrace{f \circ f \circ \dots \circ f}_{n \mathrm{\, times}} : X \to X.</math>

: This [[iterated function]] forms a [[dynamical system]]. It is often of interest in the study of such systems to find a measure ''&mu;'' on ''X'' that the map ''f'' leaves unchanged, a so-called [[invariant measure]], i.e one for which ''f''<sub>&lowast;</sub>(''&mu;'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''&mu;''.

* One can also consider [[quasi-invariant measure]]s for such a dynamical system: a measure ''<math>\mu</math>'' on ''<math>(X,\Sigma)</math>'' is called '''quasi-invariant under''' <math>f</math> if the push-forward of ''<math>\mu</math>'' by <math>f</math> is merely [[equivalence of measures|equivalent]] to the original measure ''μ'', not necessarily equal to it. A pair of measures <math>\mu, \nu</math> on the same space are equivalent if and only if <math>\forall A\in \Sigma: \ \mu(A) = 0 \iff \nu(A) = 0</math>, so <math>\mu</math> is quasi-invariant under <math>f</math> if <math>\forall A \in \Sigma: \ \mu(A) = 0 \iff f_* \mu(A) = \mu\big(f^{-1}(A)\big) = 0</math>

* Many natural probability distributions, such as the [[chi distribution]], can be obtained via this construction.


==A generalization==
In general, any [[measurable function]] can be pushed forward. The push-forward then becomes a [[linear operator]], known as the [[transfer operator]] or [[Frobenius&ndash;Perron operator]]. In finite spaces this operator typically satisfies the requirements of the [[Frobenius&ndash;Perron theorem]], and the maximal eigenvalue of the operator corresponds to the invariant measure.

The adjoint to the push-forward is the [[pullback]]; as an operator on spaces of functions on measurable spaces, it is the [[composition operator]] or [[Koopman operator]].
